# `match_one_to_many`

*preparation tool.* Pair each whole with the one set of its candidate parts whose amounts add up to it.

Use match_one_to_many to pair one whole with the several parts that make it up, such as one bank deposit with the payments it holds. Each input row is one possible (whole, part) pair, usually made by a join on a shared key and a filter on a date window. For each whole, every set of 1 to 'max_parts' of its parts is tried. When exactly one set adds up to the whole, its rows go to `matched`. Every other row goes to `rejected`, with the reason in 'reason_column'. Nothing is guessed: a whole with no answer, or more than one, is left for a person.

## Ports

- **Reads:** `candidates`
- **Gives:** `matched`, `rejected`

## Settings

| setting | type | required or default | allowed values | what it is |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `whole_key` | string | required |  | The column naming the whole on each row, such as a deposit id. |
| `part_key` | string | required |  | The column naming the part on each row, such as a payment id. |
| `whole_amount` | string | required |  | The column holding the whole's amount. A whole number or an exact Decimal. |
| `part_amount` | string | required |  | The column holding the part's amount. A whole number or an exact Decimal. |
| `max_parts` | integer | required |  | The most parts one whole may be made of. At least 1. |
| `tolerance` | number | default `0` |  | How far the parts' total may be from the whole and still add up, in the amounts' own units. 0 or more. |
| `max_candidates` | integer | default `25` |  | A whole with more candidate parts than this is not searched, and its rows are rejected. At least 1. |
| `reason_column` | string | required |  | The name of the column added to `rejected`, saying why each row is there. |

More on some settings:

- `whole_key`: For example 'deposit_id'. It must be a different column from 'part_key'.
- `part_key`: For example 'payment_id'.
- `whole_amount`: For example 'deposit_amount'. Every row of one whole must give the same amount.
- `part_amount`: For example 'payment_amount'. Every row of one part must give the same amount.
- `max_parts`: For example 3. A larger number finds bigger sets, and more ways for a whole to add up twice.
- `tolerance`: For example 0.01 to allow a cent either way. Left out, it is 0: the total must equal the whole exactly.
- `max_candidates`: Left out, it is 25. The search grows fast with the number of candidates; narrow them with a filter rather than raising this a lot.
- `reason_column`: For example 'reason'. It must be a name the input does not have.

## Notes

- No SQL operation does this. Missing values follow SQL's '=': a missing key matches nothing.
- A set adds up when the gap between its total and the whole is at most 'tolerance'. Amounts are compared exactly; nothing is rounded.
- No set adds up: every row of the whole is rejected with 'no set adds up'.
- Two or more sets add up: every row of the whole is rejected with 'more than one set adds up'.
- Exactly one set adds up: its rows are matched, and the whole's other rows are rejected with 'not in the matched set'.
- A part in the matched sets of two or more wholes: every row of each of those wholes is rejected with 'a part is claimed by more than one whole'. Nothing is tried again.
- A row missing its whole key or its part key is not a pair. It is set aside with 'missing key', even when its amount is missing too, and never counts in the amount checks below.
- A row missing its part amount is rejected with 'missing amount'. So is every row of a whole whose amount is missing on all its rows.
- Rows rejected for a missing key or amount take no part in any search, do not count towards 'max_candidates', and keep their reason whatever happens to their whole.
- A whole with more candidates than 'max_candidates' is not searched. Its rows are rejected with 'more candidates than the search allows'.
- These stop the step, naming the keys: the same whole and part on two rows; one whole with two different amounts; one part with two different amounts. A missing amount beside a value counts as different. Only rows with both keys are checked.
- Zero and negative amounts are allowed. A part of zero can join any set, so it makes a second set that adds up, if there is room for it under 'max_parts'.
- A set has at least one part: a whole of zero is never matched by an empty set.
- A Float64 amount is refused: totals of decimal-point numbers do not add up exactly. Convert it to Decimal with cast_columns first. A whole-number amount beside a Decimal one is compared by value.
- The answer does not depend on the order of the rows. Both ports keep the input order.
- An input with no rows gives two empty outputs with the right columns.

## Example 1

match each deposit to the one set of payments that adds up to it

```yaml fragment
tool: match_one_to_many
config:
  whole_key: deposit_id
  part_key: payment_id
  whole_amount: deposit_amount
  part_amount: payment_amount
  max_parts: 3
  reason_column: reason
```

Rows in:

`candidates`

| deposit_id | deposit_amount | payment_id | payment_amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 | 250.00 | A | 100.00 |
| W1 | 250.00 | B | 150.00 |
| W1 | 250.00 | E | 40.00 |
| W2 | 300.00 | C | 200.00 |
| W2 | 300.00 | D | 100.00 |
| W2 | 300.00 | F | 150.00 |
| W2 | 300.00 | G | 150.00 |
| W3 | 90.00 | H | 45.00 |
| W3 | 90.00 | I | 40.00 |

Rows out:

`matched`

| deposit_id | deposit_amount | payment_id | payment_amount |
|---|---|---|---|
| W1 | 250.00 | A | 100.00 |
| W1 | 250.00 | B | 150.00 |

`rejected`

| deposit_id | deposit_amount | payment_id | payment_amount | reason |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| W1 | 250.00 | E | 40.00 | not in the matched set |
| W2 | 300.00 | C | 200.00 | more than one set adds up |
| W2 | 300.00 | D | 100.00 | more than one set adds up |
| W2 | 300.00 | F | 150.00 | more than one set adds up |
| W2 | 300.00 | G | 150.00 | more than one set adds up |
| W3 | 90.00 | H | 45.00 | no set adds up |
| W3 | 90.00 | I | 40.00 | no set adds up |

W1 is 250.00, and only A + B adds up to it, so A and B are matched and E is left over. W2 is 300.00, which is C + D and also F + G, so nothing is guessed and all four rows are set aside. No set of W3's payments adds up to 90.00.
